title: Enterprises will run 80% of tokens through open models, but spend only 20% of budget
dek: Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two.
why: The Ollama CEO gives first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes are completely different, and the real constraint on enterprise procurement is security, not cost.
who: Founders building AI applications and agents, engineers responsible for enterprise AI procurement and architecture, and investors trying to judge the commercialization path for open models.
skip: The one-minute intro at the start and the YC recruiting plug at the end can be skipped.

points.h: The driver of open models is not saving money, it is control
points.body: Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models can solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is ‘better control over AI and customizing it for yourself’. Cost is just the part that can be solved in the short term; only after that is solved does customizing the model to your own use case come into play. The order matters: if you treat open models only as a cost-cutting tool, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption to open models, currently mainly US and European models, while also evaluating Chinese models.

points.h: Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
points.body: Ollama's cloud per-capita token usage curve has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM, and MiniMax launched in succession, and for the first time open models could support a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, customer service, marketing, and sales can all throw a hard problem at an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and fetching data along the way, consuming enormous numbers of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for this explosion.

points.h: Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
points.body: Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors before launch, but Jeff says getting a model a few weeks early counts as lucky; most of the work is crammed into the final 24 hours before launch. Three things have to be done at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, to ensure it is fast, accurate, and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are now many open-source harnesses like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the biggest growth day. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, inference layer, and application runtime all have to be glued together, a combinatorial explosion problem.

points.h: Above the token is where the new scarcity lies
points.body: Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (connecting company data and context into the model), coordination (a single request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, requiring scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgment: tokens are already in surplus, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B above the token. Following the path of cloud computing, developers ultimately prefer the best independent product at every layer, rather than a packaged Heroku or Google App Engine.

points.h: Stateful things will not sink into the model layer
points.body: Asked whether the harness will be absorbed by the model, Jeff's judgment is: the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but several categories cannot. First, the state problem — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up with the latest data, so storage is a huge independent problem space. Second, credential management and security. Open models do not come with a whole set of security tools the way closed providers do, and this is critical for enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

points.h: 80% of tokens go through open models, but only 20% of budget
points.body: Jeff's steady-state judgment: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will go through open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget flows to open models. The open-source community is driving costs extremely low, so perhaps only 10% to 20% of spending lands on open models. The hardest work stays with frontier labs, because the best researchers are there; the broad middle is done by combining open and closed models. He uses a law firm analogy: partners hand work down to a bunch of associates.

points.h: The local and cloud model mixes are not the same thing at all
points.body: On local models, US and Chinese models are basically neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a mix of US, European, and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is also clear: coding agents write code and tests, with many hard problems, mainly relying on large cloud models; end-to-end low-difficulty workflows like document processing run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router deciding when to go up to a large model.

points.h: The Flash tier of models is the precondition for unlimited tokens
points.body: Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, less than 3 months behind the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve was extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token, but low cost per task. This tier of model is good enough for 80% of tasks, fast, and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually return to that state, but it requires model architectures specifically trained for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

points.h: Two years without finding the problem is scarier than having no hype
points.body: Jeff says that when he entered YC in 2021, the direction he wrote down was ‘Kitematic for Kubernetes’ or ‘Docker Desktop for Kubernetes’, building security products like SSO for Kubernetes. The company entered YC in 2021, and Ollama did not launch until July 2023, a gap of more than two years. He says the scariest thing is not whether there is hype, but that ‘you cannot even see the north star’ — customers are usually a good north star, and not being able to see it is even scarier. The team was over 10 people at the time, and he is especially grateful to this group for sticking through several pivots.

points.h: First version in two weeks, and Llama 2 happened to launch
points.body: The trigger for the pivot was a company-wide discussion in Toronto: what would you do if you started from scratch today. They saw two problems — one was building a gateway to access any model (at the time analogized as Segment for the LLM world, i.e. the later router idea), and two, this group of ex-VMware, ex-Docker people were good at making things run, so let's make open models run. They gave themselves two weeks to build the first version, and Llama 2 launched right at the end of those two weeks, so they shipped immediately. Jeff calls this bias to action: from idea to launch in two weeks, with more users than all previous products combined.

points.h: Free and runnable anywhere took a hobbyist tool straight into the Fortune 500
points.body: Jeff says what surprised them most was the speed from hobbyists to the Fortune 500. Two reasons: open models start free, and they can run anywhere — this is extremely critical for Fortune 500 IT developer teams, because they do not need to request permission to use them. What is good for hobbyists translated directly into what is good for developers inside the enterprise. He draws a database analogy: MongoDB also went from developers to the enterprise, but LLMs are stateless, making that transition even easier than databases.

points.h: The rules of the infrastructure era fail in AI
points.body: Jeff gives two old muscle memories that must be broken. First, ‘building a layer on top of someone else is dangerous’ — this held in the infrastructure era but does not hold in the AI era; moving up the stack may actually be better, because you are closer to the customer. Second, the systems world demands that everything run exactly as designed, tested and verified, whereas LLMs by definition do not work that way — this is a feature, not a bug. He also mentions team size: some problems now do not need that many people, such as customer service pipelines, the way cloud services are delivered, and the very fact that ‘no engineer knows how all the code works’.
